misconceptions.label: Retells events out of order, or merges two episodes into one
Guesses a word from how it looks rather than from the sentence around it
Reports what a character did instead of why — literal instead of inferential
Treats a feeling as stated in the text when it has to be inferred
Picks a vivid detail as the main idea
Answers from own experience rather than from the text
Predicts without pointing to anything in the text as evidence

trees.question: What does Peter do FIRST after his mother goes out?
choices: He squeezes under the gate into Mr McGregor's garden
He is caught in the gooseberry net
He eats blackberries with his sisters
He loses both his shoes
trees.explanation: The story goes in order: he disobeys and goes under the gate, then eats, then is chased, then loses his shoes. Getting into the garden comes first.

citation.quote: But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor's garden, and squeezed under the gate!

trees.question: Retell what happens to Peter in three steps, in order.
trees.answerText: He sneaks into the garden, he eats vegetables and is spotted by Mr McGregor, and he escapes losing his shoes and jacket.
trees.explanation: Any three steps in the right order are fine — what matters is that the order matches the story.

citation.quote: Mr. McGregor was after him in no time.

trees.question: "Peter was most dreadfully frightened; he rushed all over the garden." What does 'rushed' mean here?
choices: Moved very quickly
Walked slowly
Fell over
Shouted loudly
trees.explanation: He is frightened and being chased, so 'rushed' must mean moving fast. The sentence around the word tells you.

citation.quote: Peter was most dreadfully frightened; he rushed all over the garden.

trees.question: "He was out of breath and trembling with fright." What does 'trembling' tell you about Peter's body?
trees.answerText: That he was shaking, because he was afraid.
trees.explanation: 'With fright' sits right next to the word — the sentence hands you the meaning.

citation.quote: he was out of breath and trembling with fright

trees.question: A younger reader doesn't know the word 'implored'. Teach them how to work out a word from the sentence around it, using an example from the story.
rubric: Says to read the words before and after, not just the word itself
Uses clues about what is happening or how a character feels
Gives a concrete example from the text
Does not simply say 'look it up in a dictionary'
trees.explanation: Explaining the strategy out loud is what fixes it. If you can teach it, you have it.

citation.quote: he implored her to exert herself

trees.question: Why does Peter go into Mr McGregor's garden even though his mother told him not to?
choices: He is curious and does not want to obey
The text says he was hungry and had no food
His sisters dared him to go
He is looking for his father
trees.explanation: The story never gives a reason directly — it says he was 'very naughty' and ran straight there. You infer the motive from what he does.

citation.quote: But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away

trees.question: How does Peter feel when he cannot find the gate? How do you know?
trees.answerText: Frightened and panicked — the text says he was 'most dreadfully frightened' and rushed all over the garden.
trees.explanation: Point to the words that show it. A feeling you can quote is stated; a feeling you work out is inferred.

trees.question: Teach a younger reader the difference between what a character DID and why they did it, using Peter as your example.
rubric: Names a reason or feeling behind it
Makes clear the reason is worked out, not written down word for word
Points at something in the text as the clue
trees.explanation: Separating action from motive is the whole skill of inference. Teaching it is the best way to hold onto it.

trees.question: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: Disobeying can get you into trouble
Rabbits like eating radishes
Mr McGregor keeps a large garden
Peter loses his shoes and his jacket
trees.explanation: The other three are true details from the story, but only the first is what the whole story is about.

citation.quote: Peter was not very well during the evening.

trees.question: A reader says the main idea is "Peter lost his jacket and shoes." What mistake are they making?
choices: They picked a detail instead of the main idea
They read the story out of order
They guessed a word wrongly
They used their own experience
trees.explanation: It is a real event in the story, but it is one detail. The main idea covers the whole text.

trees.question: Teach a younger reader how to tell the main idea apart from a detail. Give them a test they can use on any story.
rubric: Offers a usable test, e.g. 'does it cover the whole story or just one part?'
Gives one example of a main idea and one of a detail
Uses the story rather than speaking only in the abstract
trees.explanation: A rule the student can state in their own words is a rule they will still have next week.

citation.quote: Peter was not very well during the evening.

trees.question: Do you think Peter will go back into the garden? Give one piece of evidence from the story for your answer.
trees.answerText: Either answer is fine if it cites the text — for example, he was made ill and put to bed, which suggests he learned his lesson; or he was called 'very naughty', which suggests he might.
trees.explanation: A prediction is only as good as the evidence behind it. The claim matters less than the quote.

citation.quote: Peter was not very well during the evening.
